items.title: Rockwell Group completes Skywalker Grill at LA's Lucas Museum
items.text: Dan Howarth 26 September 2026 Here’s a closer look inside the newly opened Lucas Museum of Narrative Art , where design studio Rockwell Group has outfitted a restaurant and bar that “responds to the museum’s distinctive biomorphic architecture”. Rockwell Group ‘s Los Angeles office designed the Skywalker Grill without a single 90-degree angle, continuing the sweeping curves of the building by MAD Architects . The Skywalker Grill features no 90-degree angles to echo the Lucas Museum’s biomorphic architecture The eatery also references the warm cherry wood interiors of Skywalker Ranch, a 4,700-acre filmmaker’s retreat and workspace owned by Star Wars director George Lucas in Marin County, California. Overlooking the Los Angeles skyline, the fifth-floor restaurant and bar is named after the sci-fi media franchise’s principal character. It is open to both museum visitors and the general public for lunch and dinner. Entry to the fifth-floor space is via a corridor wrapped with cherry wood panels “Responding to the museum’s distinctive biomorphic architecture, the restaurant features no 90-degree angles,” said the Skywalker Grill team. “Curved walls are wrapped in individually crafted cherry wood panels, with no two panels alike, while finger-raked cherrywood columns echo the tambour banquettes lining the perimeter of the room.” Shimmering tiles cover the front of the snaking bar, while the back bar is clad in illuminated Corian Guests arrive via elevator to a corridor that leads to the host stand, lined on one side with cherry panelling that folds up and over the ceiling. Booths are formed with swooping partitions that organically rise and fall in height, and curve to create intimate pockets for conversation. The cherry used throughout the restaurant is a nod to the wood found at George Lucas’s Skywalker Ranch in Marin County A central island is ringed by a green crushed velvet banquette that matches the booth upholstery, and surrounded by circular tables and freestanding dining chairs in soft grey. Tamboured cherry-wrapped columns rise at slight angles and branch like tree trunks to meet the ceiling, which opens in the middle to reveal a beige plaster surface illuminated by cove lighting. A large ovoid window opens onto a terrace with panoramic views The snaking, glossy white bar counter is fronted by shimmering fluted tiles covered in crystal silver leaf, while illuminated Corian forms the back bar. A large ovoid window features operable glass panels that provide access to the outdoor terrace, where further seating enjoys views over the University of Southern California campus towards Downtown LA. “The design incorporates elements of cinematic storytelling, including framing, light, scale and atmosphere, while pairing high-tech materials with handcrafted details,” said the team. The restaurant’s American-style menu features California-grown ingredients, including Wagyu beef and honey ricotta sourced from Skywalker Ranch. Curved, undulating partitions form intimate dining booths Set in a 13-acre landscaped site near Los Angeles’ Exposition Park, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is dedicated to storytelling and features a variety of galleries, theatres and educational spaces. MAD and Stantec wrapped the building in over 1,200 curved panels, creating an extraterrestrial form that wouldn’t look out of place in one of Lucas’s beloved movies. The terrace enjoys panoramic views over Los Angeles Rockwell Group is known for its theatrical hospitality projects that immerse diners in atmospheric spaces. Other recent examples include an art deco-influenced Manhattan steakhouse , a revolving restaurant above Times Square and a “cathedral of fried chicken” . The photography is by Tom McGovern . items.title: Atelier Zébulon Perron draws on metabolism for Montreal bistro
items.text: Ben Dreith US editor 30 October 2026 Photography by Alex Lesage A monochrome palette and influences from Japanese metabolism characterise Bistrot à Franky in Montreal , Canada designed by local outfit Atelier Zébulon Perron . The restaurant is a home base for local chef Francis Blais in the city’s hip Mile End neighbourhood. Photographs Close Atelier Zébulon Perron took what it views as the standard design language of a Montreal bistro – bright lighting and lots of activity – and translated it into a more contemporary design. For studio founder Zebulon Perron, the monochrome whites and beiges, interspersed with milled aluminium accents and a large zinc bar top, allowed the studio to experiment with textures and lighting to create visual interest and contrast in the dining space. “With the monochromy of the restaurant, we experimented with textures – shiny versus matte, tile nd and stucco – and how light reacts to those surfaces in different ways,” Perron told Dezeen. The studio emphasised the postmodern and “retrofuturist” elements of the design, pointing to the custom chandeliers with their illuminated Pyrex tubes and exposed wiring, fabricated by Perron’s long-time collaborators, local lighting design studio Lambert & Fils . Perron highlighted the milled aluminium wine cellar that sits above the bar face, interspersed with portholes that are a direct reference to Japanese metabolist architecture. “There’s a postmodern, 1980s aesthetic that naturally rose from everything we were doing,” said Perron. Visitors enter the restaurant through a red-painted hallway and a metal door and handle carved from butcher block by local cabinetmaker Olivier Doray . Inside, only the terrazzo floor was a holdover from the building’s former use. Granite tabletops cover some of the larger tables, while the classic bistrot white tablecloths are draped over the smaller tables. Blond leather banquettes were placed below large mirrors on the wall opposite the bar, and these larger seating arrangements are centred by large butcher block tables, also fabricated by Doray. Custom walnut chairs were designed by local industrial designer Guillaume Sasseville . On the walls, white tile is interspersed with stucco and works of art, curated by local filmmaker Xavier Dolan . These artworks give pops of colour and Perron said that the monochromatic design elements allow both the food and the artworks to stand out in the space. “Since the canvas is pretty neutral, the food and the artwork take centre stage,” he said. A set of windows opens up the kitchen space to the dining room. Custom bar seating features white columns with seats informed by transportation design, and Perron noted that the metal details and clean lines of the bar space, as well as the metal fans, also give the interior a streamlined look. Atelier Zébulon Perron has designed some of the most interesting interior spaces in the city, including Café Constance and the dining areas for the city’s Four Seasons hotel . It also helped create the pop-up bar staged during the city’s inaugural design week earlier this year. Photography by Alex Lesage Read more Interiors Exclusives

items.title: Rotterdam’s Echo is a Tokyo-inspired listening bar
items.text: Amy Frearson Editor-at-large 30 October 2026 Photography by Sophia van den Hoek Creative director Jeﬀ Hoogendijk, DJ and producer Khalil Ryahi and architect Paul Cournet have teamed up to open a listening bar in Rotterdam , featuring a bar made from shipping crates and ombré mirrors by Sabine Marcelis . Inspired by visits to listening bars in Tokyo, the trio envisioned Echo as a flexible space that can host different events and activities, but primarily focuses on the experience of music. Located on the ground floor of Groot Handelsgebouw, a post-war office block opposite Rotterdam Centraal station, the bar has an interior designed by Cournet’s architecture and design studio, Cloud . Cournet said the idea was to adapt the concept of the listening bar to the creative energy of Rotterdam. “We wanted to make it super local,” he told Dezeen. The main bar, which functions as both a service counter and the DJ area, exemplifies this approach. Built in collaboration with Barendregt’s Kistenfabriek , a company that manufactures wooden shipping crates, together with carpenter Simon Fitskie, it’s a reminder that Rotterdam is home to Europe’s largest seaport. Its sides are printed with the words “handled with care”, which became Echo’s tagline. “We thought it would be so cool make the bar an art crate because we treated everything, from music to hospitality, as if it were art,” said Cournet. “We always wanted to do everything in the best way possible.” The space features several works by Rotterdam-based designer Marcelis , who is Cournet’s partner. Her signature ombré mirrors adorn the walls, reflecting shades of red and gold, while a linear resin lamp hangs above the bar. Polish brand Tylko supplied much of the furniture, including the modular shelving that extends across the walls to create space for displaying vinyl. Cournet previously worked with the furniture company on its Berlin showroom, a project that led to a collaboration with audio company Form Follows Frequency . Together, they developed a colourful system of speakers and subwoofers that slot precisely into Tylko’s shelving, which launched earlier this year. These speakers form part of the sound system for Echo, along with two sculptural speaker towers that stand either side of the bar. “There’s a contrast between the rawness of the exposed concrete and the more refined elements, like the sound system or Sabine’s mirrors,” said Cournet. “When you put them together, it creates a tension that I find interesting. The concrete feels a bit softer.” ECHO is one of several listening bars to have opened recently – with others including Bar Bardo in Milan and Upstairs at Hausu in London – but it is the first of its kind in Rotterdam. The space shifts from a coffee shop by day to a bar by night, and includes a curated retail offering. It can also morph to accommodate exhibitions, listening sessions of 20 to 40 people, or seated dinners for up to 40 guests. Since opening in early September, the team has invited various local record stores to contribute to the event programme. “Rotterdam has this really long history with music, with a lot of famous DJs and people who were pioneers in the music scene in the 1990s and 2000s,” added Cournet. “It feels like the project has really resonated with that community.” Photography by Sophia van den Hoek Read more Interiors

items.title: Gjergji Shkurti gives Millions Goods Ft Greene a regal renovation
items.text: Ben Dreith US editor 25 September 2026 Architect Gjergji Shkurti has collaborated with concept shop Million Goods for its second Brooklyn location, using marble, custom millwork and curated furniture to create a transition from hospitality to retail. A glossy red spiral staircase can be spotted through windows that face the buzzy part of DeKalb Street in Fort Greene, Brooklyn. The space became the Million Goods ‘s second shop after co-founder Matt Reyer, who lives nearby, spotting it when it was inhabited by a design studio. Gjergji Shkurti designed the Fort Greene outpost for Million Goods Reyer and fellow co-founder Drew Kaufmann brought on local architect Gjergji Shkurti, founder of Figure Ground , to convert the space. Whereas the original Million Goods in Greenpoint is condensed into a single level, the Fort Greene location gave the team more room to work with, with two levels and an expansive courtyard. The studio revamped a two-level space “I think this was more regal, whereas Greenpoint was a little bit more fun,” Shkurti told Dezeen, referring to the expansive Breccia Pernice stone countertop that forms the wine bar portion on the first level. Stripping the interiors back to their essentials, Shkurti organised the space to provide social areas and retail, integrating them stylistically but separating them physically, with the social spaces on the bottom floor and the retail above. Shkurti designed the space and fabricated the millwork The first-level bar and social space combines multiple different design languages into a contemporary New York style. Behind the bar, metallic speaker boxes were integrated into the custom casework, which was rendered in sapele wood finished in a peca tone. Bridge Street Sound did the sound system, integrating a large speaker directly into the face of the marble bar. Emeco bar stools by Philippe Starck line the bar, and these chairs were used with the wooden banquet seating that hems the space. A backyard takes cues from Brazilian brutalism The ceiling has a distinctly Japanese appearance, with fabric draped between wooden slats. This fabric and an additional layer of insulation were included for sound, but also, with an interesting effect, dampen the lighting from the fixtures above the fabric. A relatively large backyard space was given a central planter for a mature tree. The circular planter doubles as a bench and seating was integrated into the washed concrete walls around the space. Upstairs, a space was included for retail Shkurti said the backyard was designed to evoke Brazilian brutalism. A Louis Poulsen Flindt Plaza post is the centrepiece of the backyard space, rising from the custom pavers. The lighting company sponsored the store and its lamps and fixtures can be found throughout. The refinished facade of the historic low-rise building was refinished with the blessing of the local preservation boards, and the backyard-facing trim was given a red that aligns with the staircase in the front. In the front, the facade was kept black. The spiral staircase at the front of the shop was original, but given siding and painted a bright red by local fabricator Wood Steel Stone . Wood Steel Stone also completed an impressive central display table on the upper floor that folds aluminium and wood into ply layers with aluminium on top. Upstairs, the original wood from the floors was refinished and used. The team knocked voids in a partition wall to place speakers Shkurti’s custom millwork appears again as casing for the clothing and goods on display, which Reyer described as contemporary and accessible. Through a portal door, a metal stand, also created by Wood Steel Stone was designed to function as both a point-of-sale location and a DJ booth for events. To the sides of the portal door, voids were cleared out to put additional speakers that face into the primary retail space. Above the custom display table is a Louis Poulsen pendant lamp designed to have a vintage look. An upstairs changing area doubles as a point-of-sale station and DJ booth From the upstairs, shoppers can see kids playing basketball on courts across the street, anchoring the location in the neighbourhood. Other recent stand-out interiors include Federico Stevanovich’s studio designed with Nama Studio in Mexico City . Litening bars are increasingly a site of interesting design. Check out seven listening bars from across the globe . The photography is by Joe Thomas . Read more Interiors
